title: Western versus New York bands: rhythm and ballroom
summary: They discuss why western bands swung differently from New York bands, and Dance's theory about ballrooms versus theater shows.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Now why do you think that was? Was it purely from coming from the rhythm section?
You see, because all the bands out West played that way and I think all the
bands in New York played this way like Fletcher Henderson and Chick Webb. It was a different style altogether.
Yes, but now, Jonah Jones said to me once that they always thought of Earl Hines as a Western band.
You see, those bands of his had the same sort of, somewhat similar feeling.
Especially when they got Alvin Burroughs.
Yes. Yes, well Earl was, Earl was a Western band, but we didn't call anything Western unless it was from West or South of Kansas City. Earl had a good band.
But I think another thing, you know, another thing I think, I don't know whether you agree with it, but I have the theory that these bands from the West were mostly playing ballrooms.
And when you get bands like Earl's and Duke's in the Cotton Club and the Grend

Terrace, now they are playing shows. Now in the East there was this sort of network of theaters where all the bands were playing the Apollo and the Opera House and the Royal. And therefore there was a theatrical thing which developed which was different from the ballroom thing.
Yes, I guess so. But what I notice, even in solos there was a difference.
